title: Précision
intro: Imagine un passé différent, fais des déductions comme un détective, parle avec de vraies expressions idiomatiques et fabrique tes propres mots.

boss.name: L'Idiome Masqué
boss.taunt: Tu crois que mon examen, c'est un jeu d'enfant ? Ha ! Tu vas avoir la frousse au dernier moment, je te le garantis.
boss.defeat: Bon… c'est la goutte qui fait déborder le vase. Je m'arrête là pour aujourd'hui !

units.title: Si seulement…
units.goal: Imaginer un passé différent avec le troisième conditionnel, les conditionnels mixtes et wish / if only.

lesson.text: Tu connais déjà le conditionnel réel ([[If it rains, we'll stay home.]]) et le conditionnel imaginaire au présent ([[If I had a dog, I'd walk it every day.]]). Maintenant, on **réécrit le passé** : ce qui aurait pu arriver… mais qui n'est pas arrivé. Parfait pour les regrets !

lesson.title: Le troisième conditionnel
lesson.text: [[If]] + **past perfect**, [[would have]] + **participe passé**. [[If I had known, I would have come.]] = Si j'avais su, je serais venu. Tu peux aussi utiliser [[could have]] (aurait pu) ou [[might have]] (aurait peut-être) : [[If we had run, we could have caught the bus.]] Les deux parties peuvent s'inverser : [[I would have come if I had known.]]

head: Type
Structure
Exemple
rows: [[If I had a dog, I'd walk it every day.]]
If + had + participe, would have + participe
[[If you had called, I would have answered.]]
[[If I had slept more, I wouldn't be so tired now.]]
[[If I were braver, I would have said something.]]

lesson.text: Piège n° 1 : **jamais de would après if** ! [[If I would have known]] ✗ → [[If I had known]] ✓. C'est comme en français : « Si j'aurais su » est une faute. Piège n° 2 : dans [[If I'd known, I'd have come]], le premier [['d]] = [[had]], le deuxième = [[would]].

lesson.title: Wish et if only + past perfect
lesson.text: Pour regretter le passé : [[wish]] / [[if only]] + **past perfect**. [[I wish I had studied more.]] = J'aurais aimé étudier plus. [[If only I hadn't said that!]] = Si seulement je n'avais pas dit ça ! Rappel : pour le présent, c'est [[wish]] + passé : [[I wish I were taller.]]

reading.title: A Chain of Small Mistakes
reading.text:
Last Friday was the worst day of Olivia's school year, and it all started with a tiny mistake. The night before, she had forgotten to set her alarm clock. As a result, she overslept by almost an hour.

If she had woken up on time, she would have caught the school bus. Instead, she had to run to the city bus stop, and on the way, she tripped and dropped her lunch in a puddle. If she hadn't been in such a hurry, she probably wouldn't have fallen.

When she finally arrived at school, her class had already started the big science test. Her teacher let her write it, but she only had half the time. She did her best, but she couldn't finish. "If only I had checked my alarm!" she thought.

At lunch, she had nothing to eat, because her sandwich was still lying in a puddle somewhere near the bus stop. Luckily, her friend Ana shared her pasta with her. "If you hadn't helped me with my project last week," Ana joked, "I would have eaten it all myself!"

In the evening, Olivia told her dad about her terrible day. He smiled and said that everybody had days like that. In hindsight, Olivia realized that one small action could have changed everything. Now she checks her alarm twice every night. If she had done that from the start, she would have saved herself a lot of trouble, and a perfectly good sandwich.

questions.q: What was Olivia's first mistake?
choices: She forgot to set her alarm.

questions.q: According to the text, why did Olivia probably fall?
choices: She was looking at her phone.

questions.q: What happened with the science test?
choices: She didn't have enough time to finish it.

questions.q: What does Ana's joke suggest?
choices: Olivia had been kind to Ana before.

questions.q: What does Olivia do differently now?
choices: She checks her alarm twice every night.

questions.q: What is the main message of the story?
choices: Small mistakes can have big consequences.
You should never take the bus.
Friends should always share their lunch.

units.title: Il a dû…
units.goal: Faire des déductions et exprimer des regrets sur le passé avec must have, can't have, might have, should have et needn't have.

lesson.text: Modal + [[have]] + **participe passé** = parler du passé avec nuance. Tu peux faire des **déductions** (« il a sûrement… », « elle n'a pas pu… ») ou juger ce qui s'est passé (« tu aurais dû… »).

head: Modal
Sens
Exemple
rows: [[She must have forgotten.]] Elle a dû oublier.
[[He can't have seen us.]] Il n'a pas pu nous voir.
[[They might have missed the bus.]] Ils ont peut-être raté l'autobus.
[[You should have told me.]] Tu aurais dû me le dire.
[[I shouldn't have shouted.]] Je n'aurais pas dû crier.
c'était possible, mais ce n'est pas arrivé
[[You could have hurt yourself!]] Tu aurais pu te blesser !
c'était inutile… mais on l'a fait
[[I didn't need to wake up early.]]

lesson.title: Le piège de « il a dû »
lesson.text: En français, « Il a dû partir » a **deux sens** ! Une **déduction** : [[He must have left.]] (je suppose qu'il est parti). Une **obligation** : [[He had to leave.]] (il était obligé de partir). Avant de traduire, demande-toi : supposition ou obligation ?

lesson.title: Le contraire de must have
lesson.text: Le contraire de la déduction [[must have]] n'est **pas** [[mustn't have]], c'est [[can't have]] ou [[couldn't have]] : [[She can't have eaten the cake; she's allergic to chocolate!]]

À l'oral, [[should've]], [[could've]] et [[must've]] sonnent comme « should of »… mais on n'écrit **jamais** [[should of]] ! C'est toujours [[have]]. Autre piège : [[needn't have brought]] = je l'ai apporté pour rien ; [[didn't need to bring]] = ce n'était pas nécessaire (et souvent, je ne l'ai pas apporté).

reading.title: The Midnight Snack Mystery
reading.text:
When the Nguyen family came downstairs on Sunday morning, the kitchen was a mess. The fridge door was open, there were crumbs all over the counter, and half of Grandma's birthday cake had disappeared.

"Someone must have been very hungry last night," said Mom, looking at everyone.

"It can't have been me," said Mei. "I was at Priya's sleepover until this morning." That was true: Dad had picked her up an hour before.

Her brother Jaden looked at the floor. "It might have been the cat," he suggested. But the cat was sleeping peacefully on the sofa, and cats don't usually open fridges.

Then Dad noticed a small chocolate stain on the stairs, then another, and another. The trail led straight to Jaden's bedroom door. "Well," Dad said, "the cat must have walked very carefully up the stairs and opened your door."

Jaden's face turned red. He admitted that he had woken up at midnight, starving. "I only wanted a tiny piece," he explained, "but it was so good!"

"You should have asked us," said Mom. "And you obviously shouldn't have eaten half of Grandma's cake!"

Luckily, Grandma's party wasn't until the evening. Jaden spent the whole afternoon baking a new cake with his dad, and he cleaned up every crumb. In the end, Grandma loved it. "You needn't have made a second cake," she laughed, "but I'm very glad you did!"

choices: She was sleeping on the sofa.

choices: He really believed that the cat did it.

He was angry at the cat.
He was joking, because the clues pointed to Jaden.

questions.q: Why did Grandma say "You needn't have made a second cake"?
choices: She didn't think a new cake was necessary, but she appreciated it.
She knew that Jaden couldn't bake.
She had already bought another cake.

units.title: Les expressions (1)
units.goal: Comprendre et utiliser des expressions idiomatiques courantes comme un anglophone.

lesson.text: Une **expression idiomatique**, c'est un groupe de mots dont le sens n'a rien à voir avec les mots eux-mêmes. Si tu traduis mot à mot, c'est la catastrophe ! Souvent, il existe un équivalent en français… mais avec une autre image : [[cost an arm and a leg]] (un bras et une jambe) = coûter **les yeux de la tête**.

lesson.title: Comment les utiliser
lesson.text: Les verbes des expressions se **conjuguent** normalement : [[She spilled the beans.]] [[I'm hitting the books tonight.]] Les possessifs changent selon la personne : [[pull someone's leg]] → [[You're pulling my leg!]] D'autres sont presque figées : [[It's a piece of cake.]] [[It's not rocket science.]] [[The ball is in your court.]]

head: Expression
Mot à mot

Et ne change **aucun mot** d'une expression : [[a piece of pie]] ou [[get cold hands]], ça ne veut plus rien dire !

reading.title: Ethan's First Day
reading.text:
Ethan had just moved from Montreal to Ottawa, and on his first day at his new school, he was so nervous that he almost got cold feet at the front door. His mom smiled and told him it wasn't rocket science: all he had to do was say hello.

In his first class, the teacher asked everyone to tell a joke to break the ice. Ethan was on the fence for a moment, but then he told the funniest joke he knew. The whole class laughed, and a boy named Karim gave him a high five.

At lunch, Karim told Ethan that the math teacher gave surprise tests only once in a blue moon. "And don't worry," he added, "they're always a piece of cake." That afternoon, the math teacher announced a surprise test. Ethan looked at Karim in panic, but Karim just laughed. He had been pulling Ethan's leg: the surprise tests happened every week, and they were anything but easy.

After school, Ethan's new friends invited him to the arena. Hockey equipment can cost an arm and a leg, so Ethan only had old skates. Nobody cared. They played until the lights went off, and then they finally called it a day.

That night, Ethan was too excited to hit the sack. Moving to a new city had seemed like a disaster, but maybe it was a blessing in disguise.

choices: He had lost his new skates.

choices: He was starting to see it as something positive.
He wanted to go back to Montreal right away.
He was still afraid of his new classmates.

units.title: Fabriquer des mots
units.goal: Fabriquer de nouveaux mots avec des préfixes et des suffixes pour enrichir ton vocabulaire.

lesson.text: Avec une seule racine, tu peux fabriquer toute une famille de mots : [[happy]] → [[unhappy]], [[happiness]], [[happily]]. Les **préfixes** (au début) changent le sens ; les **suffixes** (à la fin) changent souvent la nature du mot (nom, adjectif, verbe).

lesson.title: Les préfixes
lesson.text: Contraire : [[un-]] (le plus courant : [[unfair]], [[unlucky]]), [[in-]] ([[invisible]]), [[im-]] devant m et p ([[impossible]], [[impolite]]), [[ir-]] devant r ([[irresponsible]]), [[il-]] devant l ([[illegal]], [[illogical]]), [[dis-]] ([[disagree]], [[dishonest]]). Autres : [[mis-]] = mal ([[misunderstand]]), [[re-]] = de nouveau ([[rewrite]]), [[over-]] = trop ([[overcrowded]]), [[under-]] = pas assez ([[undercooked]]).

Pièges de francophone : [[unpossible]] n'existe pas → [[impossible]] ; on ne dit pas [[unpolite]] mais [[impolite]] ; « désaccord » donne [[disagree]], jamais [[desagree]]. Et le suffixe [[-ful]] n'a qu'**un seul l** : [[helpful]], [[careful]] (jamais helpfull).

lesson.title: L'orthographe qui bouge
lesson.text: Le **y** devient **i** : [[happy]] → [[happiness]]. Le **e** final tombe souvent : [[create]] → [[creative]], [[argue]] → [[argument]] (mais [[excite]] → [[excitement]]). [[able]] → [[ability]], [[curious]] → [[curiosity]], [[strong]] → [[strength]] → [[strengthen]].

reading.title: The Kindness Club
reading.text:
When Amir started grade eight, he felt invisible. His family had just moved to Ottawa, and he found it impossible to make friends. At lunch, he usually sat alone and pretended to read.

One day, his teacher, Madame Roy, announced that the school was starting a new club. Its goal was simple: to make the school a kinder place. Amir was unsure at first, but he decided to join.

The members of the Kindness Club did small, helpful things. They wrote encouraging notes and hid them in library books. They helped younger students who were lost or unhappy. Once a month, they organized a game afternoon for anyone who felt lonely. Nothing was too small. Even a smile, Madame Roy said, could change someone's day.

At first, some students thought the club was useless. A few boys even made unkind jokes about it. But little by little, the atmosphere in the school changed. There were fewer arguments in the hallways, and more students sat together at lunch.

For Amir, the biggest improvement was personal. His shyness slowly disappeared, and he discovered an ability that he didn't know he had: he was a wonderful listener. People enjoyed talking to him, and by the end of the year, he had more friends than he could count.

Years later, Amir still remembers that club as the beginning of the most important friendship of his life. The boy who had sat next to him at the very first meeting became his best friend.

choices: Because Madame Roy gave him a prize

units.title: Articles et quantités avancés
units.goal: Savoir quand ne pas mettre d'article, parler d'un groupe avec the + adjectif et doser finement les quantités.

lesson.title: L'article zéro
lesson.text: En français, on met « le, la, les » partout. En anglais, **pas d'article** pour parler d'une chose **en général** : [[Dogs are loyal.]] (Les chiens sont fidèles.) [[I love music.]] [[Health is more important than money.]] Mais [[the]] revient dès qu'on parle de quelque chose de **précis** : [[The dogs next door bark all night.]] Pas d'article non plus dans des expressions fixes : les lieux pris pour leur **fonction** ([[at school]], [[at work]], [[at home]], [[in bed]], [[go to bed]], [[in class]]), les transports avec by ([[by bus]], [[by car]], [[by train]], mais [[on foot]]), les repas ([[have breakfast]], [[after lunch]]), les sports, les langues et les matières ([[play hockey]], [[speak French]], [[I'm good at math]]).

head: Sans article (la fonction, le général)
Avec the (un lieu, une chose précise)
rows: [[Emma is at school.]] (elle est en classe, elle étudie)
[[Her dad went to the school to meet the teacher.]] (le bâtiment)
[[Children love snow.]] (tous les enfants, la neige en général)
[[The children loved the snow at the cottage.]] (ces enfants-là, cette neige-là)

lesson.title: The + adjectif : tout un groupe
lesson.text: Pour parler d'un **groupe de personnes**, on met [[the]] + adjectif : [[the young]], [[the elderly]], [[the homeless]], [[the unemployed]], [[the injured]], [[the rich]], [[the poor]]. Deux règles : le verbe est au **pluriel** ([[The elderly are…]]) et l'adjectif ne prend **jamais de -s** (jamais « the elderlies »). Pour **une seule** personne, il faut un nom : [[an elderly man]], [[a homeless person]]. Même chose pour certaines nationalités : [[the French]], [[the British]], [[the Japanese]].

lesson.title: Few ou a few ? Little ou a little ?
lesson.text: Le petit [[a]] change tout ! [[a few]] / [[a little]] = **quelques / un peu** (positif : il y en a, ça suffit). [[few]] / [[little]] tout seuls = **peu de** (négatif : pas assez). [[few]] va avec un pluriel qu'on compte ([[friends]], [[cookies]]), [[little]] avec ce qu'on ne compte pas ([[time]], [[milk]], [[patience]]). [[We have a little time.]] = on a un peu de temps, relaxe. [[We have little time.]] = on n'a presque plus de temps, vite ! Attention : [[quite a few]] = **pas mal de**, donc beaucoup !

lesson.title: Either, neither, none… et whole ou all ?
lesson.text: Pour **deux** choses : [[either]] = l'un ou l'autre ; [[neither]] = ni l'un ni l'autre, **avec un verbe affirmatif** : [[Neither answer is correct.]] [[Neither of my parents speaks Spanish.]] (à l'écrit soigné, verbe au singulier). Si la phrase est déjà négative, c'est [[either]] : [[I don't like either of them.]] = [[I like neither of them.]] Jamais de double négation (jamais « I don't like neither »). Pour **trois ou plus** : [[none of]] ([[None of my five cousins came.]]). En paires : [[either… or]] (soit… soit), [[neither… nor]] (ni… ni). Enfin, « tout le, toute la » : [[the whole]] + nom singulier, avec l'article **devant** ([[the whole family]], [[my whole life]]), ou [[all the]] ([[all the family]]), mais jamais « the all family ». Avec un pluriel ou un indénombrable, on prend [[all]] : [[all the students]], [[all the milk]].

grammar.q: ___ is more important than money.
grammar.explain: On parle de la santé en général (indénombrable) : pas d'article. « La santé » = Health.

grammar.q: We usually go to the cottage ___.
grammar.explain: Moyen de transport : by + nom sans article (by car, by bus, by train).

grammar.q: ___ are not always happier than other people.
grammar.explain: Un groupe de personnes : the + adjectif, sans -s, avec un verbe au pluriel (The rich are).

grammar.q: Relax, there's no rush: we still have ___ time before the bus comes.
grammar.explain: Time est indénombrable et le sens est positif (pas de panique) : a little.

grammar.q: The test was so hard that ___ students passed it. Only two!
grammar.explain: Sens négatif (presque personne) avec un pluriel dénombrable : few, sans a.

grammar.q: I invited my two best friends, but ___ of them could come.
grammar.explain: Deux personnes, sens négatif avec un verbe affirmatif (could come) : neither.

grammar.q: ___ of my three cousins came to the party; they were all sick.
grammar.explain: Trois personnes ou plus : none of. Neither ne sert que pour deux.

grammar.q: It's almost midnight. Go ___!
grammar.explain: Expression fixe sans article : go to bed (on va au lit pour dormir, pas vers un lit précis).

grammar.q: The new program will help ___ find jobs more quickly.
grammar.explain: Un groupe de personnes : the + adjectif, sans -s : the unemployed.

grammar.q: There were still ___ cookies left, so I offered one to our neighbour.
grammar.explain: Quelques (positif) + pluriel dénombrable : a few.

grammar.q: I don't like ___ of these two shirts. Do you have another colour?

grammar.explain: Avec don't, on prend either ; neither ferait une double négation.

grammar.q: ___ my dad nor my uncle can cook rice properly.
grammar.explain: Ni… ni = neither… nor, avec un verbe affirmatif (can cook).

grammar.q: She spent ___ day reading in the hammock.
grammar.explain: « Toute la journée » : the whole day, l'article se place avant whole.

grammar.q: The elderlies in our building love playing cards.
grammar.explain: The + adjectif ne prend jamais de -s : the elderly.

grammar.q: The homeless needs warm clothes in winter.
grammar.explain: The homeless désigne un groupe : verbe au pluriel, need.

grammar.q: I don't like neither of these songs.

grammar.q: We ate the all pizza in ten minutes.

reading.title: The No-Waste Challenge
reading.text:
Last winter, the Nguyen family made a bold decision: for the whole month of February, they would not throw away a single crumb of food. Mom had read an article about how much food families waste, and she had been shocked.

At first, it was harder than expected. They had very few ideas for leftovers. Dad suggested soup. Mei, who is eleven, suggested pizza. In the end, they made both: leftover soup on Mondays and "fridge pizza" on Fridays, topped with whatever was left. Neither recipe looked elegant, but both tasted surprisingly good.

By the middle of the month, there was hardly any food in the garbage. The family had also realized something embarrassing: they bought far too much. Quite a few of the cans in the cupboard had never been opened. So one Saturday morning, they walked downtown, carrying three heavy bags for the food bank.

The volunteers explained that the food bank helps people of all ages: the elderly, the unemployed, students, and even families with full-time jobs who can't afford enough groceries. Mei was surprised. "I thought only the homeless needed help," she said. A volunteer smiled. "Plenty of people need a little help at some point in their lives."

At the end of February, the family looked back on the challenge. None of them wanted to go back to their old habits. Well, almost none of them. Mei's little brother admitted that he missed one thing: being allowed to leave his broccoli on his plate.

questions.q: What was the family's goal for February?
What does "Neither recipe looked elegant" mean?
choices: The two recipes did not look nice.

questions.q: What did the family do with the unopened cans?
choices: They gave them to the food bank.
They used them in the fridge pizza.
They gave them to their neighbours.

questions.q: What surprised Mei at the food bank?
choices: That the volunteers were so young
That many different kinds of people use it
That it was closed on Saturdays

questions.q: Why does Mei's little brother miss leaving his broccoli on his plate?
choices: Because the family stopped buying broccoli
Because he gave his broccoli to the food bank
Because during the challenge, he had to finish everything on his plate

questions.q: What did the family probably learn from the challenge?
choices: That pizza is healthier than soup
That food banks only help the homeless
That they should plan their shopping better
That February is the best month for cooking
